response:
Latent space curvature anisotropy refers to the phenomenon where the local geometry of a model's representation space varies directionally — some directions in embedding space are highly curved (sensitive to small input perturbations) while others are nearly flat. In fine-tuned vision-language models, this matters because fine-tuning on a narrow distribution tends to sharpen curvature along task-relevant axes while leaving orthogonal directions essentially unchanged from pretraining, creating a geometric mismatch that predicts where the model will fail: inputs that require traversing high-curvature regions generalize poorly, while inputs aligned with flat directions often generalize well but for the wrong structural reasons. The central question is whether you can measure this anisotropy cheaply — without exhaustive adversarial probing — and use it as an a priori signal of which fine-tuned capabilities are brittle versus robust. What a beginner misses is that brittleness isn't primarily about distance from training data in input space; it's about the shape of the loss landscape in representation space, so two examples equidistant from training distribution can have wildly different generalization behavior depending on the curvature of the manifold between them. The expert worry is subtler still: fine-tuning a pretrained VLM doesn't reshape the full space uniformly — it creates localized high-curvature pockets that are essentially invisible to standard validation metrics, and those pockets tend to align with semantically meaningful axes (e.g., cross-modal binding, spatial reasoning) rather than appearing as random noise, meaning they're systematically exploitable under distribution shift.
